questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 60-year-old man diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma underwent resection of Couinaud's segments II, III, and IV. What is the basis for the division of these segments?
questions.explanation:
Couinaud's segments are divided based on the distribution of the portal vein.

Veins of the liver: the portal vein collects blood from the gall bladder, pancreas, spleen, and abdominal part of the alimentary tract and transfers blood collected from these organs to the liver. Hepatic veins collect deoxygenated blood from the liver and drain directly into the inferior vena cava and ultimately into the heart.

Note: Left hemihepatectomy involves resection of segments II, III, and IV. Right hemihepatectomy involves resection of segments V, VI, VII, and VIII.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Cholecysto-vena caval line separates which of the following?

options.text: Porta hepatis and inferior vena cava
Right and left lobe of liver

questions.correctAnswerText: Right and left lobe of liver
questions.explanation:
The cholecysto-vena caval line (Cantlie line) separates the right and left lobe of the liver.

Cantlie line is an imaginary line that divides the liver into two planes. It extends from the midpoint of the gallbladder fossa at the inferior margin of the liver back to the midpoint of the inferior vena cava and contains the middle hepatic vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the cells marked in the image stores vitamin A in the liver?
questions.explanation:
Ito cells, or hepatic stellate cells, are marked as 3 in the histological image and store vitamin A. They are present in the space of Disse and are mesenchymal in origin.

They have two states. In the dormant state, they store the fat-soluble vitamin A in lipid droplets and are a significant source of growth factors involved in liver homeostasis and regeneration. In the active state, after liver injury they replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue leading to hepatic fibrosis and secrete intralobular matrix components including collagen type III (reticular) fibres.

The space of Disse lies between a hepatocyte and a sinusoid. It contains interstitial fluid, microvilli of adjacent hepatocytes and fine collagen fibres (mostly type III). Lymph produced in the liver drains through the perisinusoidal space of Disse and periportal clefts of Mall into larger lymphatics.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the liver?

options.text: Quadrate lobe is drained by the left hepatic duct
Pringle manoeuvre refers to compressing the hepatic pedicle in the free edge of lesser omentum
80% of blood supply is via portal vein
Segment IV corresponds to caudate lobe of Liver

questions.correctAnswerText: Segment IV corresponds to caudate lobe of Liver
questions.explanation:
Segment IV (left medial sector) corresponds to the quadrate lobe and not the caudate lobe (segment I). It is part of the physiological left lobe of liver (segments II, III, and IV) and is drained by the left hepatic duct.

The physiological left lobe is supplied by the left hepatic duct and left branch of the portal vein. The physiological right lobe (segments V, VI, VII, and VIII) is drained by the right hepatic duct and supplied by the right hepatic artery and right branch of the portal vein.

About 80% of blood supply to the liver is through the portal vein whereas 20% is through the hepatic artery.

Pringle's manoeuvre is compression of the hepatic pedicle at the free edge of the lesser omentum for rapid control of hemorrhage from vessels entering the porta hepatis. The lesser omentum can be divided immediately to the left of these structures and passing a tape around them through the epiploic foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The CT abdomen of a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome shows enlargement of the structure marked X in the image. Identify the structure.
questions.explanation:
The area marked in the image is the caudate lobe of the liver. Caudate lobe hypertrophy is seen in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

This segment is unique in that it receives blood supply from both the right and left portal veins and hepatic arteries. It directly drains into the inferior vena cava.

It also forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 53-year-old man presented with hematemesis and ascites. Investigations revealed the presence of a tumor at the porta hepatis causing portal hypertension. Which of the following structures is least likely to be involved by the tumor?
questions.explanation:
Hepatic veins do not enter or exit the liver at the porta hepatis and are least likely to be involved by a tumor at that location.

Porta hepatis is a deep transverse fissure on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver. Structures entering the porta hepatis include portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic nervous plexus. Structures exiting include right and left hepatic bile ducts and lymphatics.

The classical features of portal hypertension are ascites, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and distended veins around the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is referred to as Valoean sheath?

options.text: Fibrous sheath surrounding the gall bladder
Fibrous sheath surrounding the splenic vessels at hilum
Fibrous sheath surrounding hepatic artery, bile duct and portal vein in each liver segment
Fibrous sheath surrounding the pancreatic duct and CBD at the Ampulla of Vater

questions.correctAnswerText: Fibrous sheath surrounding hepatic artery, bile duct and portal vein in each liver segment
questions.explanation:
The fibrous sheath surrounding the hepatic artery, bile duct, and portal vein in each liver segment is referred to as Valoean sheath.

This is an extension of Glisson's capsule, which becomes condensed as a sheath around the branches of the portal triad structures as they enter the liver parenchyma. This arrangement facilitates surgical control of the right and left vasculo-biliary pedicles of the liver.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following pouches is seen in the gallbladder?
questions.explanation:
Hartmann's pouch is seen in the gallbladder.

Hartmann's pouch (infundibulum) is an outpouching at the junction of the neck of the gallbladder and the cystic duct. Although frequently seen, it is not a constant feature of the gallbladder and serves as a potential space where gallstones can lodge.

Option A: Pouch of Douglas or recto-uterine pouch is the most dependent part of the abdomen in the erect position in females. Option B: Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal outpouching from the developing pharynx that gives rise to the anterior pituitary. Option C: Morison's pouch or hepatorenal pouch is the most dependent part of the abdomen in the supine position and pathological fluid may collect there.

questions.question: You are a surgery resident assisting in an open cholecystectomy procedure. The senior resident asks you to ligate the structure marked in the image. Which of the following structures is it a branch of?
questions.explanation:
The marked structure is the cystic artery. It is a branch of the right hepatic artery.

The cystic artery is the main source of blood supply to the biliary system. After originating from the right hepatic artery, it passes posterior to the common hepatic duct and superior to the cystic duct at the hepatobiliary triangle. On reaching the superior aspect of the neck of the gallbladder, it divides into superficial and deep branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman was undergoing cholangiography. However, during the procedure, there was difficulty in inserting the catheter through the cystic duct. Which of the following features of the cystic duct is likely to interfere with the passage of the catheter?
questions.explanation:
Spiral valves of Heister are the mucosal folds present in the cystic duct. In most cases, they are responsible for causing difficulty in the passage of a catheter through the cystic duct.

The mucosa of the cystic duct forms 2-10 crescentic folds which are spirally arranged to form the spiral valve of Heister, also called spiral folds. These are continuous with those in the neck of the gallbladder. The function of these spiral folds is unknown but they may help to preserve the patency of this narrow, tortuous duct.

The cystic duct drains the gallbladder into the common hepatic duct. It unites with the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct.

Note: Tortuous course of the right hepatic artery, also known as Moynihan's hump or caterpillar hump, is a rare but important anomaly to recognize to prevent intraoperative vascular and biliary injuries during surgical procedures involving the liver and biliary apparatus.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. On examination, tachycardia and hypotension were present. e-FAST examination revealed intra-abdominal hemorrhage and X-ray showed fractures of the 10th and 11th ribs on the left side. Which of the following organs is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of injury to the spleen.

The spleen is a wedge-shaped organ and extends from the 10th rib to the 12th rib in the left hypochondrium. It lies along the long axis of the 11th rib and is likely to be injured in blunt trauma to the abdomen. Laceration of the spleen leads to profuse intra-abdominal bleeding and hypovolemic shock.

It is not palpable in a normal adult. For the spleen to be palpable, it has to become about three times its normal size.

Source note: The explanation notes anatomical variation in rib relation; some sources mention the 9th to 11th ribs, while Gray's Anatomy is cited as mentioning the 10th to 12th ribs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: On examination of a patient with chronic myeloid leukemia, you find his spleen has enlarged towards the right iliac fossa. Which of the following structures prevents its displacement towards the left iliac fossa?

options.text: Upper pole of the left kidney

questions.explanation:
Downward displacement of the spleen towards the left iliac fossa is prevented by the phrenicocolic ligament. Therefore the spleen usually enlarges towards the right iliac fossa.

The phrenicocolic ligament connects the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm. It is not attached to the spleen, but lies below it and supports its lower pole. When the spleen gets enlarged, the phrenicocolic ligament along with the splenic flexure restricts its downward displacement.

The phrenicocolic ligament functions as a potential barrier to spread of infection between the left paracolic gutter and the left subphrenic space.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structure is a carcinoma head of the pancreas likely to invade if it extends posteriorly?
questions.explanation:
The right renal vein forms a posterior relation of the head of the pancreas, so it may be invaded by posterior expansion of a carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.

Posterior relations of the head include right renal vein, right renal artery, inferior vena cava, common bile duct embedded in the head, right crus of the diaphragm, and termination of the right gonadal vein. Anterior relations include the first part of the duodenum and origin of the transverse mesocolon.

Relations of the neck: anteriorly the lesser sac, pylorus, and anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branch of the gastroduodenal artery; posteriorly the portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, and inferior mesenteric vein in about one-third of individuals.

Clinical note: Cancers arising from the head or neck of the pancreas are difficult to operate on because of the confluence of so many vessels near them; this also makes blood-borne spread faster.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the Ampulla of Vater in the given image.
questions.explanation:
The structure marked A in the image is the Ampulla of Vater.

The bile duct and pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) within the second part of the duodenum, which opens at the major duodenal papilla.

Sometimes an accessory pancreatic duct is present and opens into the minor duodenal papilla, about 2 cm proximal to the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

Clinical note: Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC gene defect) is associated with carcinoma of the Ampulla of Vater. Duodenal villous adenomas are commonly found around the ampulla and may be premalignant. Duodenal injuries with tissue loss distal to the major duodenal papilla and proximal to the superior mesenteric vessels are best treated in the source note by Roux-en-Y duodenojejunostomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following parts of the pancreas is devoid of peritoneum?
questions.explanation:
The entire posterior surface of the pancreas is devoid of peritoneum.

The posterior surface lies over the fascia of Toldt in front of the aorta. The splenic vein traverses directly on this surface.

Only parts of the uncinate process where the superior mesenteric vessels descend on it are also devoid of peritoneum. The entire anterior surface of the body is covered by peritoneum and the tail lies between layers of the splenorenal ligament, which is formed from peritoneum.

Note that the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ except for the tail; in that sense it is not enveloped by peritoneum, but the anterior surface is in contact with peritoneum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The arterial supply of the pancreas is mainly by branches of __________.

options.text: Right gastric, splenic and right renal arteries
Common hepatic, gastroduodenal, and splenic artery
Coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery

questions.correctAnswerText: Coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery
questions.explanation:
The arterial supply of the pancreas is mainly by branches of the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery.

Arterial supply includes anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of the gastroduodenal artery, itself a branch of the coeliac trunk); anterior and posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the superior mesenteric artery); body and tail branches of the splenic artery; dorsal pancreatic artery; great pancreatic artery; and artery to the tail of the pancreas.

Options A and C include branches of the coeliac trunk but do not include branches from the superior mesenteric artery, so they are incomplete. Right gastric and right renal arteries do not supply the pancreas.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which among the following depicts a pancreas divisum?
questions.explanation:
Pancreas divisum has been depicted in the image marked 3.

The pancreas has two ducts that normally fuse during embryological development. The accessory (dorsal) pancreatic duct of Santorini drains the upper part of the anterior portion of the pancreatic head. The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung usually runs within the substance of the gland from left to right.

When the ventral and dorsal ducts fail to fuse, pancreas divisum results. In this condition, most of the pancreas drains through a dominant dorsal duct that enters the duodenum at the minor papilla. A short ventral duct, along with the bile duct, drains to the major duodenal papilla. Therefore, major pancreatic drainage is via the dorsal duct, which opens at the minor papilla.

Patients are usually asymptomatic; however, 25-28% of these patients may experience recurrent pancreatitis that may progress to chronic pancreatitis.

Image A shows normal pancreatic ducts with communication between main and accessory ducts. Image B shows normal pancreatic ducts with no communication between main and accessory ducts. Image D shows absence of the accessory pancreatic duct.
